slides.title: Ch. 17: PDF and Word Documents
slides.sub: Documents made for people to read: pypdf for PDF files, python-docx for Word files, and what neither can do

items.body: Every output on these slides was printed by the Python above when the deck was made. The two files the book ships were fetched and hash-checked; what could not be run is marked on its slide.

slides.notes: Chapter 16 kept data in one database file that a program owns. Chapter 17 turns to the opposite case: files that other people made for other people to read, a PDF that looks the same on every screen and a Word document that opens in an editor, and asks what a program can do with them. This deck follows the chapter in its own order: the PDF package pypdf, which reads text and images, copies pages into a new file, rotates and inserts pages, lays one page over another and encrypts a file; Project 12 that combines the pages of many PDFs; the Word package python-docx, which reads paragraphs and runs, styles them, and writes paragraphs, headings, breaks and pictures; and the three practice programs, PDF Paranoia, Custom Invitations and PDF Password Breaker. It adds what the chapter leaves out and what the research found when every printed output was run again: the default encryption of pypdf is RC4 and not AES-256, the merge() line of the chapter inserts the whole file, rotations add up, insert_blank_page(2) means a width of two points, most of the attributes of Table 17-1 belong to the font and not to the run, the text of a hyperlink is in no run, a style name with a trailing space raises KeyError, the package docx cannot be imported, and the dictionary of the Password Breaker is eight times the size the page names. Everything printed on these slides was produced by Python 3.14.6, installed with uv, with pypdf 6.20.1 and python-docx 1.2.0; the programs build their own documents, and the only network use is the fetch of the two files the book ships, whose hashes are checked.

slides.title: Today's route
slides.sub: Seven parts; every range is a run of slides you can jump to

items: A PDF and what a program can do (slides 4-6)

items.label: true stories: 2 on slides, 4 in the notes
consoles and programs, all run before they were shown

slides.notes: The route has seven parts. It starts with the PDF: what a program can do with it, the memo that began the format, and the header, the table and the drawing commands that a file holds. Then reading: text page by page, the language-model clean-up that was not run, and the images of the book's own PDF. Then writing PDFs: copying pages, rotating and stamping them, and the encryption that is RC4 unless you ask for AES-256, with the life of an encrypted file. Then three projects with PDFs: combining many files, PDF Paranoia and the Password Breaker with its worst case. Then Word: a .docx file is a ZIP of XML, paragraphs and runs, and the book's demo file. The sixth part is styles and writing Word documents, ending with the invitations and with what was not run. The last part is a one-map summary and the resources. The ranges name the exact slides, so you can return to the part you need. Two of the slides are true stories and four more are told in the notes; the eight narrative diagrams of the chapter are drawn from the same specifications as the interactive page. Every output was printed by Python 3.14.6 with pypdf 6.20.1 and python-docx 1.2.0, the programs that read the book's files say so, and what could not be run is marked on its slide.
slides.take: Seven parts, from a PDF's bytes to a Word invitation.

slides.title: The questions this chapter answers
slides.sub: The chapter's own competency questions; the summary comes back to each

items: Which operations read a document, which build a new one from parts of others, and which cannot be done at all, given that PDF and Word files are made for people to read and not for programs to parse?
Which printed outputs, programs, numbers and statements of the chapter differ in current releases of the packages, in the files the book ships or in the pages it points to, and on what source?

slides.notes: The first question is the chapter's spine, and it is a question about limits. A PDF stores drawing commands that put words on a page, and a .docx file is a ZIP archive of XML parts, so a program can read the paragraphs and runs of a Word file, write a new one, copy, reorder, rotate, stamp and encrypt the pages of a PDF, and extract its text and images, but it cannot recover structure that was never stored: there are no paragraphs in a PDF, text comes out in the order it was drawn, a scanned page has no text at all and a black box drawn over words does not remove them. The second question is the watch-out of the deck. The chapter's 91 interactive statements were replayed one by one on the files the book ships under Python 3.14.6 with pypdf 6.20.1 and python-docx 1.2.0: 89 printed what the page prints and 2 differed, both in the third run of the demo paragraph. Under the versions Appendix A pins, pypdf 5.0.1 and python-docx 1.1.2, 88 matched and 3 differed. The agreement is smaller than it looks, because a statement that prints nothing cannot differ from the page, and the merge() example of the chapter is such a statement: it prints nothing and does not do what the chapter says. Each slide says where a printed line differs and on what evidence. The chips give the size of the chapter as this deck covers it: six branches, the topics beneath them, the console rows and the programs that were run, the eight diagrams, and the Python and package releases that printed every result.
slides.take: Know what a program can do with these files, and where the book's lines differ.

items.body: diagram WhatAProgramCanDoWithPdfs - SetOfUses pattern, 28 of 30 words grounded in the chapter's text

items.head: One library, three names
items.body: pyPdf (2005), PyPDF2 (2011) and pypdf are one library; a tutorial that names PdfFileReader or PdfMerger fails.

slides.notes: The use-case diagram lists what the chapter does with a PDF through one package: extract the text of the pages, extract the images of a page, copy pages into a new file, insert pages at a position, rotate pages, merge a watermark under a page, and encrypt and decrypt a file with a password. They are independent uses of the same module and not a sequence, which is why the picture is a set of uses. The console beside it shows the first trap of the chapter, which is about names. The package the chapter uses is pypdf, written in lower case, and its two classes are PdfReader and PdfWriter; PdfFileReader and PdfFileWriter, which many older tutorials use, and PdfMerger are not attributes of pypdf 6.20.1, so a program copied from such a tutorial raises AttributeError. The story is in the documentation of pypdf. Mathieu Fenniak launched pyPdf in 2005, whose last release was 1.13 in 2010; at the end of 2011 Phaseit sponsored PyPDF2 as a fork; Martin Thoma took over its maintenance in April 2022; and PyPDF2 was merged back into pypdf, all lower case and without a number. PdfMerger was removed in pypdf 5.0.0. The study found the same on ten interpreters, Python 3.11, 3.12, 3.13 and the seven releases 3.14.0 to 3.14.6, so the behaviour of these packages does not depend on the 3.x release. Two optional packages, Pillow for images and cryptography for AES, are not named by the chapter and appear on later slides.
slides.take: Use pypdf and PdfReader; the names older tutorials teach no longer exist.

slides.title: A 1991 memo called Camelot
slides.sub: Spring 1991

items.head: A page that looks the same
items.body: John Warnock, co-founder of Adobe, outlined a system called Camelot in the spring of 1991. Its goal was to capture documents from any application, send them anywhere, and view and print them on any machine.

items: 15 Jun 1993: the first Acrobat is released
A file ends with an offset and %%EOF
Its text is drawing commands, not paragraphs

items.where: Adobe Systems, in a document that outlined a system called Camelot

slides.notes: Wikipedia's article on John Warnock says that in the spring of 1991 he outlined a system called Camelot, inventing the Portable Document Format. The goal of Camelot, the article quotes, was to capture documents from any application, send electronic versions of them anywhere, and view and print them on any machine. Adobe released the first Acrobat on 15 June 1993. A PDF file made today still opens with a header line and ends with an offset and %%EOF, and its text is drawing commands that place words on a page; chapter 17 reads and rewrites exactly these files with pypdf. The account rests on these sources. Wikipedia, 'John Warnock' (spring 1991, Camelot, the quoted goal), read 2026-10-12; Wikipedia, 'Adobe Acrobat' (release 15 June 1993); this study's leaves HeaderAndTrailer and ContentStreamText. Two of the facts on the slide were read in the study itself: a small PDF written for it began with %PDF-1.4 and ended with %%EOF, and the words of its page were the drawing command BT /F1 18 Tf 72 720 Td (Page one) Tj ET. The next slide runs both.
slides.take: A PDF is a page description made to look the same on every machine.

items.body: Lines 1 to 18 of the program (the helper make_pdf(), which writes a small valid PDF 1.4 of text pages byte by byte, and the imports) are not shown. The black box is a filled rectangle drawn after the line of text.

slides.notes: The program writes a two-page PDF by hand and takes it apart with the standard library. The file starts with the header %PDF-1.4 and ends with %%EOF. The word startxref near the end gives a byte offset, and at that offset the bytes xref begin the cross-reference table, which lists the offset of every numbered object: the table of this file has 8 entries, object 0 is the free one, and the first three offsets point at the text 1 0 obj, 2 0 obj and 3 0 obj. A reader finds the table by reading the last lines, so pypdf can open a file by jumping to the end first. The words of a page are not stored as paragraphs. They are drawing commands in a content stream, BT /F1 18 Tf 72 720 Td (Page one) Tj ET, and get_contents().get_data() returns those same bytes. Two consequences follow, and both were run. Text comes out in the order of the commands and not in the order of the page: with (world) drawn first at x 200 and (Hello) drawn second at x 72, extract_text() returned worldHello, while extraction_mode='layout' returned Hello and world apart. And a black rectangle drawn over a line hides it from the eye and not from a program: extract_text() still returned Salary: 120000 USD, and the Wikipedia article on redaction says the same of PDF files. PDF 1.7 became an international standard as ISO 32000-1 in July 2008, as the Library of Congress describes it; the file the book calls Recursion_Chapter1.pdf is PDF version 1.6 made by Adobe InDesign.
slides.take: A PDF holds drawing commands, read in the order they were drawn.

slides.notes: This is the chapter's own sequence for extracting text: open the file in binary read mode, build a PdfReader, loop over reader.pages, call extract_text() on each page and add the strings, and write the text to a file; the chapter's listing falls back on pdfminer.six when pypdf cannot understand the file. The program runs the middle of it on a six-page file. Adding the strings with += gives Page 1Page 2Page 3Page 4Page 5Page 6, with nothing between the pages, which is also what happens on the shipped chapter: the last words of page 1, Al Sweigart, run into the 2 of page 2 as Al Sweigart2; joining with a newline keeps them apart. pdfminer.six returns the same text with a form feed after every page, 6 in all, and on the shipped chapter it returned 33,200 characters against pypdf's 32,981 and spaced out the chapter heading as W H A T. Layout mode keeps the horizontal gap between the columns of a table-like page, so Name and Price stay in their columns, where the default joins the words of a row with single spaces. The fallback was not needed: of eleven damaged files given to both libraries, none was read by pdfminer.six and refused by pypdf, four were refused by both. The text script the book ships, run on the sample chapter, wrote 32,981 characters in 688 lines, and printed 11 warnings that name the optional package fontTools.
slides.take: Join pages yourself, and choose the extraction mode that matches the page.

slides.title: Post-processing with AI
slides.sub: A hyphen repair by a regular expression was run; the language-model clean-up was not

items.head: NOT EXECUTED here
items.body: The chapter's section Post-Processing with AI sends extracted text to a language model to clean it. No model was called for this deck, so nothing is claimed about what one returns.

items.head: A repair that is deterministic
items.body: re.sub of a hyphen followed by a newline joins follow- and ing the execution, and it also glues well-known into wellknown. pypdf's documentation calls post-processing outside its scope.
Extracted text keeps the hyphens and row breaks of the printed page; repairing it is a separate step.

slides.notes: Extracted text keeps the hyphens and the row breaks of the printed page. A page with follow- at the end of one row and ing the execution on the next came out of pypdf with a newline between them, and re.sub of a hyphen and a newline gave following the execution. That repair is deterministic, and the console runs it, but it is not harmless: the same expression turns well-known, written over two rows, into wellknown, because a regular expression cannot tell a hyphen the typesetter added from one that belongs to the word. The chapter's own answer is a section called Post-Processing with AI, which sends the text to a language model and asks it to clean the text. That section was NOT EXECUTED in this study and is not run for this deck: no model was called, and the slide therefore claims nothing about what a model returns. The documentation of pypdf, in its page on post-processing of text extraction, says the matter is outside the scope of the library and lists dehyphenation among the steps a program takes after extraction. A scanned page raises the same question in a harder form, and the next slide runs it: it has no text to clean at all.
slides.take: Repairing extracted text is your step; the language-model way was not run.

slides.notes: The program is the chapter's loop on the file the book ships. Recursion_Chapter1.pdf has 18 pages, is not encrypted, and its first page begins 1, WHAT IS RECURSION?; the images per page, printed as separate numbers, are 7 2 1 0 0 0 1 and then zeros, and the loop writes 11 files. The file is the one the program fetches from the online materials of the third edition and checks against its sha256 before it opens a copy. The study found two differences from the page. The sample output the chapter prints says that page 7 is skipped with not enough image data, and neither the newest releases nor the versions Appendix A pins skipped it: both wrote 10_page7_Im0.tif. And the loop needs the Pillow package, which the chapter never names: without it reading an image raises ImportError, pillow is required to do image extraction, as the bare environment of the study printed. The console builds a page that is only a picture: a 40 by 40 pixel image saved as PDF has one page, extract_text() returns the empty string and the page holds one image named image.jpg whose data begins with the JPEG marker FF D8, which is what a scanned document looks like to the library. There is no text to repair and nothing to extract without optical character recognition, which pypdf does not do. An empty file raises EmptyFileError and a file cut off before its xref table raises PdfStreamError. The zip of the online materials holds the PDF and the Word file the chapter reads but not encrypted.pdf, helloworld.docx or restyled.docx, which the chapter names as files the reader makes.
slides.take: Images need Pillow, and a scan gives you images and an empty string.

items.head: A tuple is a range
items.body: (0, 5) copies five pages, (0, 5, 2) every second one, [0, 5] exactly two. A page past the end raises IndexError.

items.head: The merge() trap
items.body: The chapter's line inserts the whole file: the tuple became a bookmark title. Write pages=(0, 2).
Lines 1 to 18 of the program (the helper make_pdf(), which writes a small valid PDF 1.4 of text pages byte by byte, and the imports) are not shown.

slides.notes: The program copies pages of a six-page file into a new writer. A tuple of two numbers selects pages the way range() does, so append(file, (0, 5)) copies Page 1 to Page 5 and not the sixth, which is why the chapter's first-five-pages example works; a tuple of three adds a step, so (0, 5, 2) copies Page 1, Page 3 and Page 5; and a list names pages exactly, so [0, 5] copies Page 1 and Page 6. A page number past the end raises IndexError, Sequence index out of range, for the tuple and the list alike. merge() takes the position first and puts the copied pages there: merging the pages (0, 2) of the six-page file at position 1 of a three-page writer gave A1, Page 1, Page 2, A2, A3. Written as the chapter writes it, merge(1, file, (0, 2)), the tuple lands in the parameter outline_item, which the signature types as a title only, so pypdf made a bookmark titled (0, 2) and inserted the whole six-page file: the writer ended with 9 pages and not 5. On the shipped chapter the same line took a writer of 5 pages to 23, identically on the ten interpreters, because the file has 18; append() accepts the tuple in its second place because there the parameter may be a title or a page range. The line prints nothing, so the replay of the chapter's statements counted it as a match. Under the pinned pypdf 5.0.1 the same line raises AttributeError, tuple object has no attribute startswith. The pypdf documentation has a page on merging.
slides.take: Write pages=(0, 2) for merge(); a bare tuple becomes a bookmark title.

items.body: The chart is computed: the stored rotation after rotate(90), rotate(270), rotate(-90) and rotate(180). Lines 1 to 19 of the program (the helper make_pdf(), which writes a small valid PDF 1.4 of text pages byte by byte, and the imports) are not shown.

slides.notes: rotate() takes a multiple of 90, changes the page in place and returns it; rotate(45) raises ValueError, Rotation angle must be a multiple of 90. The angles add up and the sum is never reduced to a turn: after rotate(90), rotate(270), rotate(-90) and rotate(180) the stored rotations were 90, 360, 270 and 450, and a negative angle is stored as it was given. The chart draws these four numbers, computed again when the deck is checked. A new blank page takes its size from a page already in the writer: after pages of 300 by 400 and 100 by 100 points, insert_blank_page(index=1) made a page of 100 by 100, and add_blank_page() after a 200 by 200 page made another 200 by 200. The signature of insert_blank_page is width, height, index, so a single positional number is the width: insert_blank_page(2) made a page 2 points wide, while index=2 made a page of the normal 612 points. The chapter writes insert_blank_page(2). A watermark is a page laid over or under another with merge_page(): with over=False the watermark's drawing commands come before the page's own, MARK then BASE, so the mark lies under the text, and the default over=True puts them after, BASE then MARK. merge_page() changes the page it is called on and returns None.
slides.take: Rotation keeps adding up, and insert_blank_page(2) sets a width.

slides.title: Encrypt: RC4 is the default
slides.sub: encrypt() without an algorithm writes RC4; the chapter shows only AES-256

items.head: The chapter shows one form
items.body: encrypt('swordfish', algorithm='AES-256') wrote V 5, R 6 and a 256-bit key. Without the algorithm the file is RC4 with a 128-bit key.

items.head: AES needs a package
items.body: In an environment with pypdf alone (Python 3.14.6): DependencyError: cryptography>=3.1 is required for AES algorithm; RC4 written.

items.head: Words the chapter never uses
items.body: Pillow, cryptography and DependencyError are absent from the page; Appendix A pins pypdf 5.0.1 and python-docx 1.1.2.

slides.notes: The table is computed, not typed: for each call the program writes a one-page file, reads the document's /Encrypt dictionary back with pypdf and prints its encryption version V, its revision R and its key length. encrypt('swordfish') with no algorithm wrote RC4 with a 128-bit key, V 2 and R 3, and no crypt filter dictionary; algorithm='AES-128' wrote V 4, R 4; algorithm='AES-256' wrote V 5, R 6 and a key length of 256, which is what the chapter recommends and the only form it shows. The research also asked the command line tool qpdf, which reported AESv3 for the AES-256 file. Two optional dependencies matter in practice. AES needs the cryptography package: in the environment with pypdf alone, algorithm='AES-256' failed at encrypt() with DependencyError, cryptography>=3.1 is required for AES algorithm, while the default RC4 was written; AES-128 fails later, at write(). The images of the previous slide need Pillow. The chapter's text names neither package, and the versions the book pins are given only in Appendix A, pypdf 5.0.1 and python-docx 1.1.2, while PyPI offered pypdf 6.20.1 and python-docx 1.2.0 on the day of the study. An attempt to install the pinned Pillow 10.4.0 for Python 3.14 found no wheel and the build failed for lack of the libjpeg headers, so that environment used the newest Pillow. The pypdf documentation has a page on encryption and decryption.
slides.take: Ask for AES-256 by name, and install cryptography to get it.

items.label: program decryptCut_v1_0_0.py, lines 19 to 31 of 31

slides.notes: The state diagram follows one PDF. A plain PDF becomes an encrypted file when a writer encrypts it with a password and writes the file. A reader that opens the file is not decrypted: is_encrypted is True, and asking for pages[0] raises FileNotDecryptedError, File has not been decrypted. decrypt() returns a value that says which password matched: USER_PASSWORD for the user password, OWNER_PASSWORD for the owner password and NOT_DECRYPTED for a wrong password, an empty one or one with different capitals, and it raises nothing for a wrong password, so a program must read the returned name; the transcript runs these cases. Once decrypt() matches, the reader gives its pages, and a writer that appends them and writes a new file makes a decrypted copy. encrypt('pw') with one password sets it for both roles, so decrypt('pw') returned OWNER_PASSWORD. A file encrypted with an empty user password and another owner password opens without a decrypt() call, and the owner password still returns OWNER_PASSWORD. The program uses a blank page because the point is the password and not the text; it builds its file in memory. The study also ran pdftotext without the password, which refused the encrypted file, and with it, which read it; that is the research's observation of a second program and is not repeated here.
slides.take: decrypt() returns which password matched; read it, because it never raises.

items.body: diagram CombiningManyPdfs - Workflow pattern, 26 of 30 words grounded in the chapter's text

slides.notes: Project 12 is the chapter's first program built from steps: find all the PDF files of the working directory, sort their names without regard to case, open each one, copy every page after the first into one writer and save the result. The activity diagram has one choice, whether another file is left, and the program follows it. Three corrections come from the study. As printed, the loop appends to pdf_files, a name never defined, and Python 3.14.6 answers NameError: name 'pdf_files' is not defined, suggesting pdf_filenames; the shipped combine_pdfs.py is not the finished program either, because it writes PdfWriter without the pypdf prefix and stops at NameError. The test filename.endswith('.pdf') misses a file named with capitals, which is why the program here lower-cases the name, and the file c.PDF is found. And the program does not guard against reading its own output: a second run found combined.pdf in the folder and read it as one of its inputs, so the 3 pages of the first run became 5 here (the research's own run went from 5 pages to 9). Sorting with key=str.lower puts A.pdf before b.pdf, as the diagram says. With the name corrected the program combined three small files into combined.pdf with every page but the first of each.
slides.take: Guard Project 12 against its own output, and test file names in lower case.

slides.notes: The third practice program decrypts a PDF by trying every word of a dictionary, in lower case and in upper case, until decrypt() stops returning NOT_DECRYPTED. The program here uses a four-word dictionary so that it can run in a blink: the password is CHERRY, found on the sixth attempt, after apple, APPLE, banana, BANANA, cherry; a dictionary of n words costs up to 2n attempts, 8 for four words. The chapter's file is another size. The dictionary.txt of the online materials has 349,900 lines, all lower-case letters, between 4 and 12 letters long, which is 8.0 times the 44,000 words the page names, so trying both forms of every line is 699,800 attempts and not the 88,000 of the page. The worst case, a password that is not in the list, was run to the end on a file written by pypdf 6.20.1: it found nothing and took 241.7 seconds for RC4, the default of encrypt(), and 1,467.5 seconds for AES-256, the two runs started together on a machine with two cores. A stronger algorithm costs about six times as much per guess, so the chapter's remark that a long random password defeats the program is shown by the timing and not only stated. The password swordfish, which the chapter uses for its examples, is not in the dictionary. Both numbers are single runs on one machine on 12 October 2026, they vary with the machine, and they are not repeated by any check of the deck.
slides.take: A long, random password beats a dictionary; AES-256 makes each guess dearer.

slides.title: A .docx file is a ZIP of XML
slides.sub: 14 February 1989

items.head: PK, for Phil Katz
items.body: Phil Katz of PKWARE and Gary Conway designed the ZIP format; its first release is dated 14 February 1989. Office Open XML is extended from it.

items.head: python-docx, imported as docx
items.body: The package docx (0.2.4, 6 Feb 2014) fails on import in Python 3.14.6: ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'exceptions'.

items.who: Phil Katz of PKWARE and Gary Conway of Infinity Design Concepts
items.where: PKWARE, Inc., in the dispute with Systems Enhancement Associates over the ARC format

slides.notes: Wikipedia's article on the ZIP file format gives 14 February 1989 as the initial release and says the format was designed by Phil Katz of PKWARE and Gary Conway of Infinity Design Concepts, after Systems Enhancement Associates sued PKWARE over its archiving products. The first two bytes of a ZIP file are usually PK, the initials of Phil Katz. Office Open XML is one of the formats listed as extended from ZIP. In this study a new python-docx document began with the bytes PK and held 17 parts, among them word/document.xml, which is why a .docx file can be opened with the zipfile module. The account rests on these sources. Wikipedia, 'ZIP (file format)' (history, the initials PK, initial release 14 February 1989, Office Open XML among the formats extended from it), read 2026-10-12; this study's leaves DocxIsZipOfXml and DocumentXmlBody. The console shows it: a new python-docx document saved to memory begins with the bytes PK, holds 17 parts, and one of them is word/document.xml, whose body for one paragraph is <w:p><w:r><w:t>Hello, world!</w:t></w:r></w:p>, a paragraph (w:p) that holds runs (w:r), each holding text (w:t). That is why a .docx file can be opened with the zipfile module, and why paragraphs and runs are the two words of the Word half of the chapter. The format is a published standard: Wikipedia gives 7 December 2006 as the first release of Office Open XML, as Ecma standard ECMA-376, and November 2008 for the four-part International Standard ISO/IEC 29500, after a fast-track process that ended in April 2008. In the study the template that docx.Document() starts from still named python-docx as its author and the year 2013, had no paragraphs, one section and 164 styles. The chapter says to install Python-Docx, not Docx, and to write import docx. The page of the docx project on PyPI shows version 0.2.4 as its latest release, dated 6 February 2014, still offering pip install docx; the study installed it in Python 3.14.6 and the import failed with ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'exceptions', a module of Python 2, and this build ran that import again and got the same line. The working package, python-docx, was at version 1.2.0, released on 16 June 2025.
slides.take: A .docx file is a ZIP of XML; install python-docx, then import docx.

slides.notes: These six branches are the route of the deck. The PDF format comes first: a header, objects, a table and a trailer; text that is drawing commands in stream order; and text that a box does not remove. Reading PDFs follows: the pages of a PdfReader start at index 0, layout mode reads the page by its columns, and images are read from a page. Writing PDFs: a tuple is a page range, rotation adds up, and AES-256 needs a package. Word documents: a docx file is a ZIP archive of XML, a paragraph holds runs, and a style has an exact name. Writing Word documents: headings have levels 0 to 9, bold has three states, and a picture is added from a width. The last branch is tools and practice: install python-docx and import docx, Project 12 joins the pages, and a dictionary is tried in both cases. Together they answer the first question of the chapter, what a program can do with documents made for people, and the slides that say where a printed line differs answer the second. The map is drawn from the same specification as the interactive page.

The textbook chapter is free to read online and holds every listing of the chapter; the documentation of pypdf and of python-docx describe the two packages. The reference links are the pages for the topics where the deck corrected the chapter: encryption, merging, the post-processing of extracted text and styles; the rest of the fifty-odd sources of the research, among them the PDF standard itself, the pages on images and watermarks, pdfminer.six and qpdf, are in the research package. Two of them are slides, the Camelot memo of 1991 and the ZIP format of 1989; the other four were told in the notes: the Office Open XML standard, Ecma in 2006 and ISO in 2008, on the slide of the ZIP archive; the PDF standard ISO 32000-1 of July 2008 on the slide of the file structure; the four names of the library on the slide of what a program can do; and the package docx that cannot be imported on the slide of the ZIP archive.

slides.notes: Four claims, each carried by a result you saw printed. If you can say them in your own words and run the examples yourself, you have the chapter. The console rows use only documents made in memory, so they can be typed into any Python that has pypdf, python-docx and Pillow; the programs build their own documents, and the two that read the book's files fetch them and check their hash first. The rows were run again under Python 3.14.6 with pypdf 6.20.1 and python-docx 1.2.0 each time the deck was built, and the programs were run again by the check that compares the slides with the recording. What was not run is marked on its slide: the language-model clean-up, Microsoft Word and a PDF viewer. The next chapter of the book works with CSV, JSON and XML files, where a program reads data that people and other programs wrote in plain text, and what this chapter taught about formats, optional packages and the difference between a file made to be read and a file made to be parsed carries over.
